Butterfly In Ellipse

GeometryCurvesConstructions
Game: This is a picture to explore: dots on an oval make a crossed shape, and more dots sit on a straight line where its sides cross it.
How to play: Drag any dot on the oval or on the straight line, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press Check the theorem to test what you see.
4
Look for the math

Drag a dot on the oval and five of the six dots on the line stay exactly where they were. The last side of the shape quietly swings around to keep the sixth crossing too. That is the butterfly porism.

A crossed four-sided figure

With four dots A, B, C, D on the conic, the sides are DA, AB, BC, CD — the shape crosses itself like a butterfly. Each side meets the straight line at one dot: F da, F ab, F bc, F cd. Make a new four-dot shape and keep three of those crossings. The page says the fourth side must still cross the line at the fourth dot. The logic test builds hundreds of such pictures by the applet's own rule and finds the fourth crossing in every well-behaved case.

Why Pascal's hexagon proves it

Take the six dots A, B, C, A', B', C'. By Pascal's theorem, the crossings of the opposite pairs AB with A'B', BC with B'C', and AC with A'C' all lie on one line — and the first two are F ab and F bc. A second hexagon A, D, C, A', D', C' puts AC ∩ A'C' and CD ∩ C'D' = F cd on the same line, so AD and A'D' meet there too. Since AD already passes through F da, so does A'D'. That is the whole theorem.

Why the oval's shape does not matter

The proof only asks which lines cross where, never how far apart the dots are. Such statements are projective, so a proof for a circle works for every proper conic. In test form: stretch a circle by x → 200 + 1.4x, y → 150 + 0.8y (an affine map) and the crossings still match. The applet draws an ellipse by stretching a unit circle the same way: a dot at angle t becomes (cx + A cos t, cy + B sin t), and the code uses that map for every intersection.

More sides, and an even number

The page says the number four can be replaced by any even number, and the applet lets you choose 4 to 20 sides. The test checks 6, 8, 10 and 20 sides: after dragging a vertex, each side still meets the line at its own dot. It also checks 5 sides and finds the claim fails there — the even-number qualification is real, not decoration. When a side is almost parallel to the line its crossing runs far off the board and the applet's own |det| < 1 guard returns no point; the page does not cover that degenerate case.

Try this: turn on names, drag A a long way around the oval, then press Check the theorem. Now press + twice to make an eight-sided butterfly and drag one vertex again.
